To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a family of quasi‐equilibrium probability densities, parametrized by a set of macroscopic variables, is employed as a nonequilibrium statistical model of Hamiltonian dynam-ical systems; (2) an optimization principle is developed to estimate the evolution of the macroscopic state by optimizing over paths in this family of densities; and (3) the closed reduced equations for the mean resolved vector are derived by Hamilton‐Jacobi theory, and the value function for this principle is identified

(a) the evolution of the macroscopic state is determined as the solution of a Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation that is the Euler-Lagrange equation for the optimization principle; (b) the cost function for this optimization is the lack-of-fit functional that measures how well the reduced model approximates the microscopic dynamics; (c) the weights that enter into this cost function are the closure parameters of the reduced model; (d) these closure parameters can be adjusted to fit experimental data or to

the best-fit reduced model of a Hamiltonian dynamical system is a model of nonequilibrium thermodynamic form, and the closure parameter in the reduced equations is the reciprocal of a weighted, ensemble-averaged kinetic energy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a general method for deriving nonequilibrium statistical models of Hamiltonian dynamics.
the development of a systematic approach for deriving closed reduced equations of motion that describe nonequilibrium statistical behavior of Hamiltonian dynam- ical systems.
the problem of finding the best-fit macroscopic model that describes the evolution of a set of resolved macroscopic variables.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimization principle is an efficient and systematic way of deriving closed reduced nonequilibrium statistical models of Hamiltonian dynamics.
the optimization principle is a general and powerful method for deriving reduced models of Hamiltoniansystems, with nonequilibrium thermodynamic properties.

the optimization principle provides a systematic and unified approach to nonequilibrium statistical modeling of Hamiltonian dynamics, and the resulting reduced equations are consistent with the principles of nonequilibrium thermodynamic theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optimization principle provides a general method for deriving nonequilibrium statistical models of Hamiltonian dynamics.
the general optimization principle for deriving nonequilibrium models of Hamiltonian dynamics is a variational formulation of the principle of least action.
the method of optimization over statistical models provides a general, systematic, and unified approach to nonequilibrium thermodynamic modeling of Hamiltonian dynamics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the closure parameter is a function of the resolved variables, and it can be calculated by the optimization procedure.
the closure parameter in nonequilibrium statistical models can be systematically optimized to fit the microscopic dynamics of the underlying Hamiltonian system.
the best-fit reduced model is a nonequilibrium statistical mechanics of the resolved variables that satisfies the second law of thermodynamics.
